memory_leads.lead: Managed canal/chokepoint transit has a multi-actor control chain distinct from ordinary open-sea navigation: vessel/master and operator, local ship agent, transit authority or traffic control, pilots or other mandated navigation services, and commercial voyage planning must align before a passage becomes executable.

Reservation, booking or transit-slot state can be a separate capacity allocation layer from physical channel capacity. A vessel may be technically capable of transit yet commercially or administratively unready because the usable passage opportunity has not been secured.

Arrival timing around a booked or expected transit window creates a synchronization problem: ETA updates, required notice, lateness or premature arrival can change queue position, service sequencing or waiting time even without a formal closure.

Anchorage or pre-transit queue is an inventory of vessel-days. Queue growth converts infrastructure congestion directly into effective-capacity absorption because ships remain unavailable for productive voyage progress while waiting.

Some managed passages use convoy, directional traffic, lane, meeting-point or other sequencing logic. The structural point is that safe throughput can depend on coordinated batches and traffic direction rather than simple first-come continuous flow.

Lock-based canals add staged chamber/lockage readiness and possible intermediate waiting states. Transit time can therefore include multiple serial infrastructure queues rather than one entrance queue.

Draft, beam, length, air-draft or other dimensional limits can determine whether a vessel can use a managed passage at all or only under restricted loading. The important memory category is voyage-route eligibility, not a specific canal limit.

Water level can turn nominal canal geometry into a time-varying capacity constraint. Lower allowable draft can reduce cargo carried per transit, require loading adjustments or divert vessels, so the bottleneck can affect both voyage count and payload efficiency.

Transit tolls and associated service charges form a route-cost state that must be compared with alternative-route fuel, time, charter and schedule costs; exact tariff schedules and historical charges are deferred to Evidence.

Transit clearance includes administrative and financial readiness such as required declarations, agent coordination, fee/payment or guarantee arrangements and authority acceptance. Physical arrival alone does not imply permission to enter the managed passage.

Priority, service-class or auction-like allocation mechanisms can exist as generic capacity-management structures, but blind recall is not reliable enough to retain any canal-specific class, eligibility rule or pricing mechanism without Evidence.

Rerouting is a threshold decision rather than an automatic reaction to delay: operators compare uncertain queue/transit time, route eligibility, tolls, fuel, cargo commitments, charter consequences and downstream schedule value against the alternative route.

A missed transit opportunity can propagate nonlinearly: one lost slot or queue delay may force later convoy/lock sequencing, invalidate downstream berth or connection plans, increase fuel for schedule recovery and absorb additional vessel-days beyond the initial wait.

The atlas chokepoint theme should distinguish geopolitical or physical closure from managed-capacity friction. Booking scarcity, queues, sequencing and draft/water restrictions can create large effective-capacity effects without the route being closed.

The atlas tonne-mile theme is refined because chokepoint eligibility and queue economics can trigger discrete rerouting; the resulting extra distance is an operational decision produced by managed transit conditions, not only geography or geopolitics.

P024 route-duration uncertainty should separate environmental uncertainty from managed-infrastructure uncertainty: weather may alter ETA into the canal, while the canal's booking, queue and water state determines whether that arrival converts into passage.

P022 port-call waiting and P025 chokepoint waiting are analytically similar vessel-day sinks but should remain separate operational states because the actors, readiness gates and downstream alternatives differ.

The broad idea that Suez, Panama and other chokepoints can change voyage distance and effective capacity is already present in the atlas; P025 retains only the operational allocation/readiness mechanics.

Generic pilotage, traffic-control and marine-service readiness was already captured in P022; P025 includes those actors only where they are part of a managed transit sequence rather than as another port-service catalog.
